1878–1958 · United States

John B. Watson

American psychologist and founder of behaviourism. He argued that psychology should study only observable behaviour and applied conditioning to human emotions in the controversial Little Albert case.

Biography

John Broadus Watson was born in 1878 in Travelers Rest, South Carolina, into a poor family. His father left home when he was a teenager. He studied at Furman University and took his doctorate at the University of Chicago in 1903 with a study of learning in rats. In 1908 he moved to Johns Hopkins University and in 1915 he was president of the American Psychological Association.

In 1920 he had to leave the university over the scandal of his relationship with his research assistant, Rosalie Rayner, whom he later married. He went into advertising at the J. Walter Thompson agency, where he was very successful. He continued to write popular books. He died in 1958 in New York.

Questions he investigated

  • Can psychology be a natural science like biology, without relying on introspection?
  • How do animals learn to find their way and solve tasks?
  • Are human fears learnt?

Contributions

In 1913 he published the article "Psychology as the behaviorist views it", regarded as the manifesto of behaviourism. He argued that psychology should abandon the study of consciousness and introspection, and deal only with observable behaviour, with the aim of predicting and controlling it.

Inspired by Pavlov, in 1920 he published with Rosalie Rayner the study of Little Albert, an eleven-month-old baby who was conditioned to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise. The fear seemed to spread to other furry objects. The case was cited for decades as evidence that emotions can be learnt.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

Watson built on the work of Ivan Pavlov and Edward Thorndike. His approach dominated American psychology for decades, and B. F. Skinner developed it differently as radical behaviourism. Mary Cover Jones, a student of Watson's, showed in 1924 with the case of a boy named Peter that a childhood fear could be removed.

A documented anecdote

In Behaviorism (1925) he wrote his most famous line: "Give me a dozen healthy infants [...] and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist". The next sentence is rarely quoted: he admitted he was "going beyond my facts", adding that advocates of the contrary view had been doing so for thousands of years.

Criticism, limits and reception

The Little Albert study had serious problems: a single baby, loose measurements and no documented attempt to remove the fear created. Today it would be ethically unacceptable. His child-rearing advice, which recommended not kissing or hugging children, was heavily criticised and research on attachment refuted it.

His insistence on objective methods did leave a lasting mark: much of today's scientific psychology measures behaviour, even though it no longer refuses to study mental processes.

References

  1. Watson, J. B. (1913). Psychology as the behaviorist views it. Psychological Review, 20(2), 158–177.
  2. Watson, J. B. y Rayner, R. (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 3(1), 1–14.
  3. Buckley, K. W. (1989). Mechanical man: John Broadus Watson and the beginnings of behaviorism. Nueva York: Guilford Press.
